subject: Agriculture
title: China's South-North Water Transfer
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: China's South-North Water Transfer.

hook.text: Southern China has abundant water. Northern China—where the wheat grows—is running dry.

buildup.text: China is building canals to transfer 45 billion cubic meters of water per year from south to north.

discovery.text: Three routes span thousands of kilometers. The eastern route follows the ancient Grand Canal alignment.

twist.text: The project costs over $80 billion and displaces hundreds of thousands of people from reservoir areas.

climax.text: Critics say conservation and efficiency could solve the problem without moving a single drop.

punchline.text: Move mountains or save water? China chose to move the rivers.

quiz.question: How much water will China's South-North Transfer project move annually?

details.summary: China's South-North Water Transfer Project is the world's most ambitious interbasin water diversion, moving water from the Yangtze River to the arid north. This topic covers the project's three routes, engineering challenges, and debate over its environmental and social impact.
details.whyItMatters: Northern China faces severe water scarcity while producing much of the nation's grain. This $80 billion project attempts to solve a crisis that threatens food security for hundreds of millions of people.
takeaways: The project's three routes span over 4,500 kilometers when combined
It transfers billions of cubic meters of water annually from the wet south to the dry north
Hundreds of thousands of people were relocated to make way for construction

faq.question: What is China's South-North Water Transfer Project?
faq.answer: It is a massive infrastructure project with three routes—eastern, central, and western—that diverts water from the Yangtze River basin northward to Beijing, Tianjin, and the drought-prone North China Plain where water scarcity is acute.

faq.question: What are the criticisms of the South-North Water Transfer?
faq.answer: Critics point to massive costs (over $80 billion), displacement of hundreds of thousands of people, ecological damage to donor river systems, pollution of transferred water, and the argument that demand reduction would be more effective.
